procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment of the High Court dated 03.07.2012, specifically the part setting aside the sentence of imprisonment under Sections 328, 392, and 307 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) and modifying the fine from Rs. 2000/- to Rs. 30,000/-.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The respondent-accused filed Criminal Appeal No. 79 of 2003 in the High Court. The High Court decided the appeal on 03.07.2012, upholding the conviction but modifying the sentence by setting aside the imprisonment and increasing the fine.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The State of Himachal Pradesh filed a Special Leave Petition (SLP) under Article 136 of the Constitution, which was converted into Criminal Appeal No. 667 of 2017, challenging the High Court's modification of the sentence. The respondent did not challenge the part of the High Court's judgment upholding the conviction.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was permitted, in law, to do away with the punishment of imprisonment altogether and substitutes the same with fine alone?

facts: The High Court, while hearing an appeal, affirmed the conviction of the accused as decided by the trial court.
However, the High Court modified the sentence by completely removing the punishment of imprisonment and substituting it with only a fine of Rs. 30,000.
law: The relevant sections of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) for the offenses (e.g., Sections 307, 328, 392) prescribe a punishment of imprisonment 'and' a fine, using the language 'and shall also be liable to fine'.
Under Section 386 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.), an appellate court has the power to alter the nature or extent of a sentence when upholding a conviction.
This power to alter a sentence must be exercised in accordance with the provisions of the penal code under which the accused was convicted and cannot be used in a manner contrary to the law.
application: The Supreme Court interpreted the word 'and' and the phrase 'and shall also be liable to fine' in the relevant IPC sections to mean that both imprisonment and a fine are mandatory components of the punishment.
It reasoned that for these specific offenses, awarding a punishment of imprisonment is a must, and a sentence cannot consist of only a fine.

The Court determined that while the High Court has the power to alter a sentence under Section 386 Cr.P.C., this power does not extend to imposing a sentence that violates the mandatory requirements of the IPC.
By completely removing the imprisonment part of the sentence, the High Court acted contrary to the law.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court committed a clear legal error and its approach was 'impermissible in law'. The High Court was not permitted to do away with the mandatory punishment of imprisonment and substitute it with a fine alone, as the relevant statutes required both imprisonment and a fine to be imposed.

issue.issue_text: Whether, the High Court in exercise of its appellate jurisdiction under Section 386 of the Code could have set-aside the sentence of imprisonment, as imposed by trial court under Section 328, 392 and 307 IPC by enhancing the amount of fine to Rs. 30,000/- from the fine Rs. 2,000/- as ordered by trial court.

facts: The respondent was convicted by a trial court for offenses under Sections 328, 392, and 307 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC).
The trial court sentenced her to two years of imprisonment for each offense (to run concurrently) and a fine of Rs. 2,000.
On appeal, the High Court upheld the conviction but set aside the entire sentence of imprisonment.
The High Court substituted the imprisonment sentence with an enhanced fine of Rs. 30,000.
law: Under Section 386 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.), an appellate court has the power to alter the nature or extent of a sentence.
However, this power must be exercised in accordance with the sentencing provisions of the specific law under which the accused was convicted (in this case, the IPC).
The power to alter a sentence does not extend to exercising powers contrary to the law or the statutory scheme.
The language of Sections 307, 328, and 392 of the IPC specifies a punishment of imprisonment 'and' a fine, making a term of imprisonment a mandatory component of the sentence.
application: The Supreme Court examined the relevant sections of the IPC and determined that for offenses under Sections 307, 328, and 392, awarding a punishment of imprisonment is a must.
The Court found that the High Court's action of completely removing the imprisonment sentence was "impermissible in law" because it violated the mandatory sentencing requirements of the IPC.
The Court clarified that while the High Court could have reduced the length of the prison sentence, it could not eliminate it altogether.
The Court characterized the High Court's decision not as a permissible "alteration" of the sentence, but as an erroneous "reversal" or setting aside of the legally required punishment.

The Court also noted that the trial court had already considered the respondent's mitigating circumstances (being a woman with children) and had taken a lenient view, so there was no justification for the High Court to show further mercy by removing the mandatory imprisonment.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's decision, holding that the High Court committed a legal error and exceeded its powers under Section 386 Cr.P.C. by setting aside a mandatory sentence of imprisonment and substituting it with only a fine.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was permitted, in law, to do away with the punishment of imprisonment altogether and substitutes the same with fine alone?
appellant_arguments: The appellant (the State) questioned the validity, propriety, and justification of the High Court's order which set aside the sentence of imprisonment and substituted it with a fine.
respondent_arguments: The respondent-accused argued that the High Court rightly set aside the sentence of imprisonment and enhanced the fine in view of the facts and circumstances of the case.
The respondent, being a lady who had to look after three minor sons (two of whom are mentally unsound), argued that the sentence of imprisonment was rightly set-aside.
The respondent contended that the High Court's judgment was just and equitable and should not be interfered with.

arguments.issue_text: Whether, the High Court in exercise of its appellate jurisdiction under Section 386 of the Code could have set-aside the sentence of imprisonment, as imposed by trial court under Section 328, 392 and 307 IPC by enhancing the amount of fine to Rs. 30,000/- from the fine Rs. 2,000/- as ordered by trial court.
appellant_arguments: The appellant (the State) challenged the High Court's decision to set aside the sentence of imprisonment for serious offenses and substitute it with an enhanced fine, questioning its validity, propriety, and justification.
respondent_arguments: The respondent-accused argued that the High Court's decision was correct and justified by the mitigating circumstances of the case.
The specific circumstances cited were that the respondent is a lady responsible for caring for her three minor sons, two of whom are mentally unsound.
The respondent argued that the High Court's order was just and equitable and did not warrant interference.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An appellate court's power to alter the nature or extent of a sentence must be exercised in accordance with the scheme of punishment as provided for in the Penal Code.
obiter: When a matter is within the discretion of the court, it is to be exercised according to well-established principles.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Appellate Court cannot exercise its power under Section 386(b)(iii) of the Code to alter a sentence of imprisonment and fine into a sentence of only a fine, as doing so is contrary to the statutory scheme. Conceding such a power to an appellate authority would lead to unfair and unjust consequences, particularly where the underlying offenses mandate imprisonment.
legal_tests_applied: When determining the quantum of a sentence, the court's discretion must be governed by reason and fair play, not by whim and caprice. The discretion must be exercised to impose an adequate sentence that protects society and responds to the collective conscience.

An appellate court's power to alter a sentence under Section 386(b)(iii) cannot be exercised in a way that contravenes the punishment prescribed by the statute for the offense for which the accused has been convicted.
policy_considerations: Allowing offenders who are financially well-off to get away with only a fine for serious crimes would be counterproductive and against the interest of society.
Justice demands that courts impose punishment befitting the crime to reflect public abhorrence. The court must consider the rights of the victim and society at large, not just the criminal.
Imposing an inadequate sentence out of undue sympathy does more harm to the justice system by undermining public confidence in the efficacy of the law.

It is the duty of the court to impose an adequate sentence to protect society and deter the criminal. A liberal attitude of imposing meager sentences is against the interest of society, which needs to be strengthened by the deterrent effect of the sentencing system.
